content.content:
# The record and the report

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

If you have findings or decisions, put them in your report in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## The gap ledger

Each row is one claim. It has a status (`POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`), a class (`implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`) and how to reproduce it. The rows are under sections by area.

The rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

Reports everywhere cite rows by number. So never renumber or move a row. Give a new issue a new row with a new number. Close a fixed row in place.

The ledger is large: whole, it is about 400K tokens, and one row can be 12K characters. Never read it whole, and never print whole matching lines from it. To find rows, run the `ledger-find` query with a few words (below). If it reports many more rows, add a word. Then print each row that you need with `ledger:ROW`.

## FACTS and POSITIONS

FACTS and POSITIONS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry goes in `FACTS-history.md` and `POSITIONS-history.md`.

A FACTS entry is the fact, its source and its test in a few lines, under a bold title. It points to the report that holds the detail.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a history walk from `HEAD` stops early. A `git log` of a directory is useless here. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. Do not read the big files whole. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh
    $T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'            # the FACTS.md entry whose bold title holds them
    $T 'section:HEADING'             # every FACTS.md entry of a section
    $T 'ledger-find:WORDS'           # each ledger row that holds every word: number, status, claim's start
    $T 'ledger:424'                  # one row of the gap ledger
    $T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'  # one of the curator's decisions
    $T 'index:WORDS'                 # the INDEX.md lines on a topic, one per note
    $T 'map:README.md#Touch this'    # a section of a note under explorations/coordinator/map/
    $T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'            # a section of any note, or of a .tex chapter
    $T --check ...                   # where each key matches and its size; --part N continues; --help

Cite a FACTS entry by its bold title, or by its opening words if it has no title.

## Writing to the record

- Add a fact to FACTS in the commit that establishes it. A decision of the curator enters POSITIONS in the next commit after the curator states it.
- Rewrite a wrong line of FACTS or POSITIONS in place.
- Write each thing in one place. The curator's words are written once, in POSITIONS. Everything else points there.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a standalone note there, write its INDEX line.

## Practices

- Cite a measurement that your brief cites or that your own work took, with its source. Take it again only if the code changed under it, and then say what changed.
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.
----
# Committing and pushing

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go, on the branch that you work on, and push that branch (below).

Scratch includes logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs and lists. Your tree's `tmp/` is gitignored. A private caches folder outside `tmp/` is not.

## What to commit

- Commit the Fortress change and its tests, your report if it is a file, and a reusable script.
- Commit your lines for the ledger, FACTS or the plan with your work (`records.md`, "Writing to the record").
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`.
- Do not commit a copyrighted PDF or deck. `research/decks/` is gitignored. Cite such a source by its Wayback URL. `research/extracts/` holds our own summaries, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.

## How to commit

- Commit as you go, each commit in one command. Never commit a directory copy, and never use `git add -A`:

      git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- Other agents may have uncommitted edits in the same tree. The command above commits none of them. Leave them alone.
- Before you commit a staged change of more than a few hundred lines, read `git diff --cached --stat`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer the harness suggests. If the work moves to another session, `explorations/protocol.md` gives the new session line.

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, do not push. That agent pushes right after it commits, so look again shortly. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push twice, in this order:

         git push origin main
         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8

     The second push keeps current the branch that the container is re-provisioned from (the `cloud-container` skill, a lost container).
- Push no other branch unless your brief names it.

# Plan: microGPT compiled on the JVM

The order Pavol approved on 2026-09-26 (`coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-26, the plan). The evidence under it is the inventory `coordinator/open-items-2026-09-26.md`.

## Where we stand, 2026-09-26

- **Runs.** microGPT runs under walk. Both check programs pass 40 of 40 from an empty cache (inventory B3).
- **Stops.** On the compiled path, all 18 of microGPT's components stop at name resolution. The compiler's own library has no `Array`, `Char`, `ImmutableArray` or `Vector`. This has not moved since the baseline, and it is expected: the fix is the switch-over, not new names in the compiler's library (inventory B3).
- **Decided.** One library, the interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks (09-21). The exclusion rule is kept and the number tower flattened, with walk taught coercion first (route A, 09-24). Sizes get a descriptor at run time (design B, 09-24). The array design comes after the switch-over.
- **Landed.** Batches 1 to 4. Batch 4 taught walk coercion, taught the compiled checker `nat` and `int` sizes, and fixed the `ZZ32` shift count. The checker reports 125 errors on the interpreter's library (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-4/RECORD.md`).
- **Decided, not built.** The specification rung S (S1 and S2 answered on 09-26); the wrapping operators ∔ ∸ ⨰, then rung O's overflow check; the run-time size rung; the flattening.

## The principle for the batches

Every batch lands with the specification, the library and both paths agreeing. So the work is grouped by what has to change together, not split finer.

Two rules of the batch machinery shape the order: two rungs in one batch may not change the same declaration, and a rung cannot build on another rung of its own batch, since every rung branches from the batch's base (`coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:465`, batch rule 1). That is why the wrapping operators and the flattening sit in different batches, and why rung O's check follows the operators.

How a phase-3 batch's content is chosen (the coordinator's method, as batch 10 was planned): the measure is the distance, the compiled checker's errors on the one library, and the source is the last landed gate's per-site list (`compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`), every error with its site and class. The planner, an Opus worker, sorts it into three piles: (1) decided and free to fix, the library's one-off slips and the checker's defects with a known fix, which go into the batch; (2) waiting on a decision of Pavol's or a judgement (after batch 9: the arrays, 98, after the switch-over by his answer to batch 8's Q4; the self-typed bodies, 30, a list of ways and a judgement first; `isLeftZero` and items 37 to 42, his), which are held and listed in the record; (3) waiting on a probe, which is probed before the record is written (P1 for row 424's F-bounded half). Pile 1 gains the defects the last review routed as owed, the items this plan queues ("a checker rung after batch 8"), and his decisions ready to build (item 20). The pile is cut into rungs by code area, no two rungs on one declaration and none building on another (the two rules above), usually four, since one landing pays for them all and the harness runs two agents at once. Fable reviews the record in place; a question goes to Pavol only where a pile-2 item needs his word. There is no target size and no target cost per error: the planner takes what of pile 1 fits the rungs (batch 10: 148 of the 340, 192 held).

The comparisons on a range's index type parameter in the generic range bodies (row 600, eighteen sites of the distance): `checkSelection`'s `>` and `<` on `I` (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:129`, `:133`), `Range.CMP`'s `SCMP` and the `FORWARD_CMP` bodies (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3826`, `:3879`, `:3912`, `:3937`, `:3964-3965` at `fa14a190c`), `CompactFullRange`'s `|self|` (`:3974-3976` there) and `TrivialOpenRange`'s methods (`:3856-3862` there; each a line lower since climb batch 9's rung R); walk dispatches each at run time. The three repairs are his choice under POSITIONS, "Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only": move the bodies to the `ZZ32` types of rank 1 to 3; declare generic `PCMP`/`SCMP`; or compare through a bound. No default on record; needed before the switch-over for phase 3's distance. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-range-meets/REPORT.md:222` (section 6), `SKEPTIC.md:175` (section 8).

41. `#0`, `#(0,n)` and `#(0,n,m)` (row 601, three sites of the distance): `extent1Range`, `extent2Range` and `extent3Range` declare `ExtentRange[\…\]` and answer an empty full range for a zero extent, and the rank-2 and rank-3 forms write its bounds out of order, so `|#(0,3)|` is 1 (`Library/RangeInternals.fss:1513`, `:1522`). Repairing the order changes that value to 0, a value walk prints, which needs his word; the declared type could become `RangeWithExtent[\…\]` (and `opr #`'s with it), or a zero extent could answer an empty extent range. Default: left, today's values pinned by `ProjectFortress/tests/RangeDeclarations.fss`. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-range-meets/REPORT.md:229` (section 6), `SKEPTIC.md:174` (section 8).

42. `String`'s `left` and `right` answer the character itself although they declare `Maybe[\Char\]` (row 606; `Library/FortressLibrary.fss:4165-4166`, api `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2419-2420`): with `get` declared on `String` the checker reads 'Function body has type OR(Char,Nothing[\Char\]), but declared return type is Maybe[\Char\]', two sites of the distance. His choice: answer `Just` as `Range` and `List` do, a value walk prints changed, or declare the type the bodies answer. No default on record; today's values are pinned by `ProjectFortress/tests/StringPieces.fss`. Needed before the switch-over for phase 3's distance. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-string-slips/REPORT.md:187` (section 12).

Before the switch-over, raised by climb batch 10 (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-10/RECORD.md`):

43. The one library's tuple comparisons and `LexicographicOrder` compare values of an unbounded type parameter (row 634, 18 sites of the distance): a bound such as `StandardPartialOrder` refuses what walk compares today, a pair of pairs among them, and `List[\E\]` extends `LexicographicOrder` at every element type; the text compares lists whose elements support the comparison and is silent on tuples. The fork: a `where` clause or conditional member the checker reads, or bounds that give up nested tuples and lists of unordered elements. No default on record; it bears on phase 3's true zero. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-number-order-slips/REPORT.md:101` (section 5).

44. `QQ`'s `ceiling` and `truncate` are declared `ZZ` and return the rational itself for ±∞ and 0/0 (row 635, two sites of the distance): the text types them ℤ (`Specification/basic-lib/numbers.tex`, section "Rational Numbers") and says in the next paragraph that they return the argument. The fork: declare ℚ, throw at an infinity, or keep ℤ with the paragraph changed. No default on record; the library follows the paragraph today, pinned by `ProjectFortress/tests/NumberOrderListDeclarations.fss`. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-number-order-slips/REPORT.md:103` (section 5).

45. Library code reads a size or an index from a value typed `Generator`, which declares neither, and `Indexed`'s default `indexValuePairs` answers a `Generator` (row 629, nine sites of the distance). The ways weighed by climb batch 10's rung G: count by a reduction, which changes the cost of `|self|`; `bounds` for `indices`, which changes the count where the indices are a subset of the bounds; or `indices` and the relational targets declared `Indexed`, which retypes `List`, `Set`, `PureList`, `Sparse` and the generators of generators. Each is a redesign, not a slip. No default on record; it bears on phase 3's true zero. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-generator-slips/REPORT.md:158` (section 8), `:226` (section 14).

46. `__bigOperator2`'s fused arm answers `I0` where `O0` is declared (row 632, one site of the distance, uncovered by climb batch 10's rung G's repair of the arm's call): widen the typecase pattern to `BigOperator[\I0,O0,I0,L0\]`, which types the arm and changes when the compiled path fuses an outer operator whose `O` differs from its `I`, or leave it with the row. The worker, both skeptics and the judge leave it to him. No default on record. Evidence: `compile-ladder/rung-generator-slips/REPORT.md:161` (section 8), `:229` (section 14), `JUDGE.md:144` (section 6).

A local function whose parameter type, or parameter and result types, are left out crashes the compiled checker three ways (rows 620 to 622: 'Type is not inferred', 'TryChecker returned an untyped expr', 'Result of typechecking still contains intermediate nodes'), where the compiled path refuses the same omission at top level or in a method, 'Missing parameter type for x' (row 405), and the text leaves the inference of omitted types undescribed (`Specification/basic/inference.tex`, the chapter's opening). # P1: an F-bounded type parameter that nothing at a call fixes, under walk: the judgement

## For Pavol

**Question.** Under walk, what does a type parameter get when no argument fixes it and its bound names the parameter itself, as `T` in `SUM`'s `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]`? Today it gets `Bottom`, so `SUM[i <- 1:n] i` dies at its first element. Twelve ways are on file, six measured. Which one?

**Refresher.**

- A type parameter is a hole in a declaration that a type fills: `T` in `opr SUM[\T\]()`. Its bound is the widest type allowed in the hole. `T extends Number` says: any number type.
- An F-bound is a bound that names the parameter itself: `T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]`. It says: `T` must be a type whose `+` takes a `T` and gives a `T`. `ZZ32` fits, `RR64` fits, `Number` does not, since `Number` has no `+` of its own. The library's algebra is written this way (`AdditiveGroup[\T\]`, `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`, `StandardMin[\T\]`, `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:262`, `:274`, `:189`), because in Fortress an operation on a type is declared on that type, `ZZ32 + ZZ32`, not on a parent, `Number + Number`. The bound is what lets the checker accept `a + b` inside `SUM`'s own code.
- "Nothing at a call fixes it." A call usually fills the hole from its arguments: `SUM (1#100)` has a generator of `ZZ32`, so `T` is `ZZ32`. But the clause form `SUM[i <- 1#100] i` is rewritten by the parser into a call of `SUM()` with no argument, made before any element exists (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:1302`, `__bigOperator` takes the reduction first). Nothing fills the hole.
- Your decision on record for that case: the parameter takes its bound. For an F-bound there is no bound to take: `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` is not a type until `T` is known. The paper the rule comes from leaves this case out: "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md:282-285`).
- One line: `total = SUM[i <- 1#100] i` (`explorations/claude_demo.fss:33`). Today: "Unification error: Closure/Constructor for join param 1 (a:BOTTOM) got arg 98: ZZ32". Written `SUM[\ZZ32\][i <- 1#100] i`, it runs.
- Who meets it. The specification's five red examples, each this shape: `opr (n: ZZ32)! = PROD[i <- 1:n] i` (`SpecData/examples/preliminaries/Overview.factorial.fss`, `advanced/OprDecl.Postfix.fss`), `factorial(n) = PROD[i <- 1:n] i` (`preliminaries/Overview.Expression.big.fss`), `SUM[i <- x.indices()] x[i] DOT y[i]` (`advanced/OprDecl.Bracketing.fss`), `SUM [x <- 1#100] 3 x + 2` (`advanced/Generators.ReductionClass.fss`). The walk smoke test. 18 of the team's 21 demos, which are not gated. The library itself: `String`'s `upto` and `beyond` call `BIG MIN` with nothing written (`FortressLibrary.fss:4237`, `:4243`), and run only because `MinReduction`'s join is typed `Any`, not `T` (row 424's last note; row 628). MicroGPT does not meet it: its walk checks write every argument (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlatCheck.fss:27`, `:56`, `:72`), and `microgpt2.fss` hides the library's `SUM` with its own (`:257`).

**The nine steps, in short.**

1. The type theory. An F-bound `T <: F[T]` has many solutions (`ZZ32`, `RR64`, every type that extends `AdditiveGroup` of itself) and no largest one: generics are invariant, so the solutions are not ordered, and "the bound" as one type does not exist (by reading; the notion is Canning, Cook, Hill, Olthoff and Mitchell, "F-bounded polymorphism for object-oriented programming", FPCA 1989, cited by its record). `Bottom` is the one closed type that fits every F-bound, and it holds no value: a hole filled with nothing. The paper's rule, the intersection of the upper bounds, is stated only where no bound names the parameter (`ParkPOPL2019-extract.md:196-205`, `:282-285`). So the theory gives no instance here. It leaves three honest answers: refuse the call, keep the hole abstract, or read the type from somewhere else, the elements or a default.
2. What each path does today. Walk: `Bottom`. Rung W gives a parameter nothing fixes its bound, but `boundAtInstances` answers null for a bound that mentions the parameter, and a big operator's static parameters are kept at `Bottom` on purpose (`EvaluatorBase.java:140-144`, `:156-188` at `cec70988b`; rung W's decision D2). Walk then checks the first element against `join(a: T, b: T)` at `T = BOTTOM` and refuses it (`NonPrimitive.java:256-269`); an empty sum takes the identity witness's first branch and `cast[\BOTTOM\]` fails with `CastError` (`FortressLibrary.fss:3208-3215`, `:33-37`). The compiled checker: the bound, and it refuses the call, "an F-bounded parameter that nothing fixes has no instance at its bound" (rung I's report, section 5, `BIG MIN`'s no-argument form; row 425 for the clause form).
3. What the specification says. Normative: a reduction is rewritten by the type `N` of its expression, `SUM[\N\]` with `SumReduction[\N\]` (`defining-generators.tex:154-164`). So `SUM[i <- 1:n] i` means `SUM[\ZZ32\]`. The inference chapter: a parameter nothing fixes takes the intersection of its upper bounds, "never ... at `BottomType`" (`inference.tex:93-105`), and it lists "the element type of a reduction that only its generator clauses determine" as not yet described: the rule gives the big operator's parameter "its bounds, not the type of the elements" (`:240-249`). Its interpreter box records walk's `Bottom` as a departure (`:285-289`). The revival's note in the reductions chapter: until an implementation rewrites by type, write the argument (`reductions.tex:27-44`).
4. Where it sits in the type system. Three places. (a) The rewriting, which picks `SUM[\N\]` from the expression's static type: walk has no static types. (b) The instantiation of the call `SUM()`: where walk decides today, before any element exists. (c) The typed sites inside the reduction, `join(a: T, b: T)`, `result: T := red.empty()` (`RangeInternals.fss:1104`), the identity witness: walk checks each against the run-time value in hand. Under walk the element type can only come from (c).
5. What the library does in the same family. Every device of its own says: under walk, keep the parameter out of the way and let the elements' own types do the work. `AssociativeReduction` joins `simpleJoin(a: Any, b: Any)` and lifts to `AnyMaybe`, which is what keeps `BIG MIN` and `BIG MAX` running at `Bottom` (row 628; the checker refuses those 13 sites). The comprehensions collect into `AnyCovColl` and build the collection at the elements' type (`CovariantCollection.fss:144`); giving them the bound instead broke six tests in batch 9 (D2's evidence: `ArrayList[\Object\]` refused where `List[\Number\]` was declared). `__bigOperator2` has `__resolveBottomArgumentType`, after the team's comment "This is too strong when I0 is BOTTOM" (`FortressLibrary.fss:1337-1340` at `cec70988b`). The 2012 `SumReduction` was typed `Number`, "Hack to permit any Number to work non-parametrically", which your answer 7 removed. The team's tests write the argument where the element type is a type variable, 16 lines, and leave 158 clause forms unwritten.
6. What the peers do (read now at the URLs cited in the judgement's step 6 below). Static languages refuse: C# (CS0411, "cannot be inferred from the usage"), Rust (E0282, "type annotations needed"), and the compiled checker. Scala takes the minimal solution, `Nothing`: walk's `Bottom`. Java keeps the hole abstract: a fresh type variable whose bound is the F-bound with itself substituted (JLS §18.4); such a variable admits no value but `null` (by reading), so a `join` typed in it is as closed as walk's. Haskell defaults an ambiguous numeric type to `Integer` then `Double` (Report §4.3.4): way 1's idea, limited to the numeric classes. Julia, the one dynamic peer, reads the type from the elements; on an empty collection it needs `init`, the identity, unless it can infer the neutral element, else "reducing over an empty collection is not allowed". Walk is dynamic; its peer is Julia.
7. What the commits say. The team ran the big operators at `Bottom` under walk and wrote the library around it (step 5). The revival: answer 7 removed the `Number` hack (rung F, `d846e3644`) and the 21 demos stopped; the chapter's rule and its box (rung T); the checker's bound (rung I, batch 8); walk's plain-bound half (rung W, `669b77d03`, batch 9), with D2 keeping big operators at `Bottom`; the probe (`fd2c6ea10`). Nobody has built the type-directed rewriting on either path (rows 424, 425).
8. The derivation from your decisions. "Takes its bound, never `Bottom`": the letter cannot apply, there is no bound to take; the spirit applies, a parameter that nothing fixes must not refuse every value. "The examples join the gate at zero red, not respelled" rules out writing the argument and refusing. "Custodians": the team's own practice under walk is the elements' types with the parameter out of the way. "Fast code": walk is not timed and this question has no speed side; the compiled path keeps its refusal until row 425's rewriting is built, which no way here touches.
9. The ways (the probe's numbering), each with what it does, what it touches, what it costs.
   - 1, a default, `ZZ32`: walk gives the parameter the identity witness's first type. One edit in `instanceOf`. Breaks every sum of floats: `SumR` and 14 of the 18 demos die at `join param (a:ZZ32) got arg ... Float`. Out on the evidence.
   - 2, the bare form, `SUM (1#100)`: runs today; covers only a body that is the variable itself. Not a fix.
   - 3, the elements' type read at run time: cannot be built where walk instantiates, since the reduction exists before any element does. Way 11 is its nearest realisation.
   - 4, the library keeps `T` out of `SumReduction`'s typed sites, as `BIG MIN`'s reduction does: a library edit in the opposite direction of row 628, which wants those sites typed for the checker. Not measured.
   - 5, the 2012 `Number` catch-all: your answer 7 removed it.
   - 6, write the argument: the examples are not respelled (your decision); the smoke test and 18 demos would each be edited, which R10 holds ("Let's not touch them").
   - 7, the specification's type-directed rewriting: needs static types; the compiled path's road (row 425), not walk's.
   - 8, `Bottom`, today: the five examples red.
   - 9, `Any`: one block in `instanceOf`, about 20 lines. Smoke test, 14 of 18 demos and the three tests green; the suite unchanged but for the flipped test. One visible change: a set comprehension's collection becomes `NodeSet[\Any\]` where today it is `NodeSet[\Int\]`. Generics are invariant, so by reading a binding `s: Set[\ZZ32\] = { ... }` is then refused: the shape that broke six tests in batch 9. No gated test has it for sets.
   - 10, the bound read without `T` (`AnyAdditiveGroup` for `SUM`, `Any` for `PROD`, `Object` for `BIG MIN`): about 60 lines that evaluate the bound at `Bottom`. The same verdicts as 9, `NodeSet[\Object\]`, and the answer depends on how the library's placeholder traits happen to be written; walk has no intersection types to do better.
   - 11, the parameter left open (`OPEN`): a type of walk's own, below every type as `Bottom` is, that every value matches wherever walk checks a value against a type. About 60 lines in five interpreter files. The same verdicts as 9. It keeps today's types where today runs (`NodeSet[\Int\]`), and gives `6 : Int` as the written `SUM[\ZZ32\]` does and `3.0 : Float` for a sum of floats (as a written `SUM[\RR64\]` would, by reading). Where a program prints the type of an F-bounded generic's result, it prints `OPEN`.
   - 12, refuse, as the checker does: about 25 lines. The smoke test, all 18 demos, the team tests `simpleSum` and `setSum`, and the library's own `upto` and `beyond` are refused; the five examples stay red.

**Recommendation.** Way 11: walk does not instantiate an F-bounded parameter that nothing fixes; it leaves it open, and the reduction runs on its elements' own types.

**What a yes commits you to.**

- A walk rung in batch 11: the open type, about 60 Java lines in five interpreter files, no library line, no model line.
- Two passages of the specification rewritten in the revision form: the inference chapter's interpreter box and the reductions chapter's note, with their Appendix I entries.
- One expected-failure test promoted, one gated test added, one new expected failure with its ledger row: an unwritten empty reduction over a type other than `ZZ32` gets `ZZ32`'s identity under walk (`0 : Int` for an empty sum of `RR64`). Every way measured has this limit; only the written argument or the compiled path's rewriting removes it.
- `ant testSpecData` joins the gate once its five examples are green, as your decision says: about 90 s with its build, less inside a gate that has already built.
- The 18 demos and the smoke test run once and reported, none edited; by the probe, 14 and the smoke test run to the end, and 4 stop later where answer 8 makes a `ZZ64` divided by a float explicit.
- Row 424 closed; the skill's two lines on it, and the walk example (once the root `CLAUDE.md`'s, now the skill's `interpreter.md:43`) back to `explorations/claude_demo.fss` as PLAN's batch 11 line says; the skill lines at your word to the skill writer.
- A program meant for the compiled path still writes its argument (row 425 stays).
- A name: walk will show a type called `OPEN` in the rare place a program prints such a type. You may want another word.

**What a no costs.**

- Way 9 instead: the same green with a smaller edit, but the comprehension's collection changes type under invariance, by reading the D2 shape; a gated test would be needed to see it break.
- Way 12 or nothing: the five examples stay red, your gate decision is not met, and under 12 the library's own `upto` is refused.

## The judgement

### 1. The way, stated

An F-bounded type parameter that nothing at a call fixes is not instantiated under walk. It is left open.

- "Open" is a type of walk's own (`BottomType.OPEN` in `plan-9/probes/P1-open.patch`). It is below every type, as `BottomType` is (`BottomType.java:20-22`, `subtypeOf` answers true), so it sits wherever `Bottom` sat: the identity witness's `typecase` over `() -> T` still takes its `ZZ32` branch, and `BigReduction[\OPEN,OPEN\]` matches `__bigOperator`'s parameter as `BigReduction[\BOTTOM,BOTTOM\]` did. Nothing but itself is below it (`FType.java:312-318`, the fallback `other instanceof BottomType`).
- Every value matches it where walk checks a value against a type: a closure's parameter (`NonPrimitive.java:256`, through `typeMatch`, `FType.java:108`, which `OPEN` overrides), a typed local (`LHSEvaluator.java:219`), `as` and `asif` (`Evaluator.java:104`, `:113`) and a `typecase` clause (`:1396`). So `join(a: OPEN, b: OPEN)` admits the elements, `result : T := red.empty()` admits the identity, and `cast[\OPEN\](v)` returns `v`.
- It applies at instantiation only (rung W's D1), to any generic function whose parameter's bound mentions the parameter and that nothing fixes, big operators included: the probe's block tests `bounded`, not `bounds`, so D2's exclusion of big operators does not reach it, and a big operator's plain-bounded parameters stay at `Bottom` (probe `List`, `ArrayList[\Int\]` in every column).
- What it is, by reading: the run-time counterpart of the specification's type-directed rewriting. The chapter picks `SUM[\N\]` from the expression's static type; walk, with no static types, leaves the hole open and lets each typed site take the element in hand. It is also the sum-replacement judgement's alternative 2, "a parameter whose type erased to Bottom accepting any argument", named there as walk's road if one is wanted (`reviews/sum-replacement-judgement.md:282-289`).
- What it is not: an instance. The chapter's "never `BottomType`" and the paper's "never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom" are about an instance that refuses every value. An open parameter refuses none. The specification's box says so in those words, not as "the parameter takes `OPEN`".

### 2. Against each alternative

- Against 9 (`Any`) and 10 (the bound without `T`): the same measured verdicts, and a smaller edit for 9. What decides is the one measured difference and its reading. Under `Any` the set comprehension of probe `Set` builds `NodeSet[\Any\]`, under 10 `NodeSet[\Object\]`, under `OPEN` and today `NodeSet[\Int\]` (`P1.md`, the probes table). Generics are invariant (the skill's language section; the chapter), so `NodeSet[\Any\]` is not a `Set[\ZZ32\]`, and a typed binding or a parameter `Set[\ZZ32\]` refuses it. The record has the measured analogue: D2's candidate (a) gave `BIG <||>` and the map comprehensions their bound, and six tests broke on exactly that refusal (`rung-walk-instance/decision-record.md:46-51`). Ways 9 and 10 do to the F-bounded comprehensions (`BIG {}`, `BIG UNION`) what (a) did to the plain-bounded ones; no gated test has the shape for sets, which is why the probe's suite pass did not show it. Way 11 keeps the elements' type by construction. Second, 10's answer depends on whether a placeholder trait exists for the bound (`AnyAdditiveGroup` yes, one narrowest for `MultiplicativeRing` no): a rule that changes when the library adds a trait. Third, under 9 and 10 the instance does not meet its own bound; walk never checks a static argument against its bound (`EvalType.bindGenericParameters`, by the probe), so nothing refuses it, but the chapter would have to say that walk takes a type that does not satisfy the declaration. "Not instantiated" is the sentence that is true.
- Against 1 (`ZZ32`): 14 of 18 demos and `SumR` die at a `Float` where the parameter is `ZZ32`. Haskell's defaulting works because it applies after the elements' types are known; here it applies before.
- Against 12 (refuse): the library's own `upto` and `beyond` are refused through 13 demos (`FortressLibrary.fss:4237`, `:4243`), the team tests `simpleSum` and `setSum` lose their passing verdicts, and the five examples stay red against POSITIONS, "The specification's examples join the gate at zero red". The checker's refusal is right for a path with static types, where the rewriting by `N` is the fix (row 425); walk has no such fix to wait for.
- Against 6 (write the argument): the same decision ("the examples are not respelled for walk") and R10's hold on the demos. It stays the rule for a program meant for the compiled path, and the reductions chapter's note keeps saying so for that path.
- Against 4 and 5 (library devices): 5 is reversed by answer 7; 4 would untype `SumReduction` while row 628 asks the opposite, the reductions typed at `R` so the checker accepts them. Under way 11, by reading, row 628's repair runs: `simpleJoin(a: R, b: R)` at `R = OPEN` admits the elements, which it did not at `Bottom`. So 11 unblocks the library's typing instead of adding another untyped site.
- Against 7 (the rewriting by `N`) and 3 (the elements' type at instantiation): not buildable where walk instantiates. 11 is their shadow.
- Against 2 and 8: not fixes.

### 3. The work for batch 11

The batch script's rung W block already names the shape of this work "Under P1" (`explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js:150-152`); this section fills it in.

- The rung: walk, one rung, the interpreter area. The edit is the probe's `P1-open.patch` against `cec70988b`, re-read on batch 11's base, since batch 10 landed since (`ec718967a`): `EvaluatorBase.java` (`instanceOf`'s F-bounded block, `mentionsItself`, the open instance, rung W's trace with its D8 switch), `types/BottomType.java` (`OPEN`, its `typeMatch` and `toString`), `types/FType.java` (the `subtypeOf` fallback), `Evaluator.java` (three checks), `LHSEvaluator.java` (one check).   - `ProjectFortress/tests/XXXUnwrittenSumRungF.fss` promoted by `git mv` to a plain name by its topic. Its three assertions (`emptySum(0)` is `0`, `SUM[j <- 0#4] j` is `6`, `PROD[j <- 1#3] j` is `6`) hold under way 11 by the probe (`SumEmptyZ`, `SumZ`, `Prod`).
  - One gated test of the open parameter, by reading from the probes, every value asserted: `SUM[j <- 0#4] (j / 2.0)` is `3.0`; `PROD[j <- 1#0] j` is `1`; `BIG MIN[j <- 0#4] (j - 2)` is `-2` and `BIG MAX` `1`; a set comprehension bound to a variable declared `Set[\ZZ32\]` and its size (the shape that separates 11 from 9 and 10); a plain generic `mk[\T extends Cmp[\T\]\](): BoxU[\T\]` called as `mk()` and its result used; `"ab.c".upto('.')`. The team tests `simpleSum.fss` and `setSum.fss` keep their verdicts (the probe: rc 0 under 11).
  - One expected failure for the kept limit, with a new ledger row (home: the interpreter, class implementation gap): `emptyRSum(n: ZZ32): RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#n] (j / 2.0)` at `n = 0` asserted to be `0.0`; under every way measured it is `0 : Int` (`P1.md`, "The empty sums and products"), walk returning it without a check. The fix is the compiled path's rewriting by `N`, or a reduction's identity read from its generator, neither this rung's.
  - `BIG MINMAX[i <- 0#4] i` with nothing written, measured first (row 424's batch-10 note: an `InterpreterBug` at `Bottom`); gated as a plain test if it runs at `OPEN`, as an expected failure if not.
- The five examples: `ant testSpecData` run once on the rung's tree, as the FACTS entry ran it. By reading all five go green: each fails today for the one cause the smoke test fails for (FACTS, "`ant testSpecData` runs 130 ..."), and the smoke test, `SumZ` and `Prod` run under way 11. content.content:
- **Forks are probed before a batch is briefed.** "if there are known decision forks, which we can evaluate using probes, we should be doing these during this phase, during this planning phase": a fork a probe can settle is probed first, so that the decision is his and the worker gets a clean task, never a decision left to a worker and reviewed after the fact. Rows are taken one per message with refreshers (other languages, what makes sense in a high-performance language), not in groups.
- **A brief describes the problem, not the solution.** "How do we prevent the myopic view? … I want to have full creativity of solutions": a worker that has not read our notes lists every way the language and the library offer before a design choice reaches him; a rule that blocks an option is answered with how the library gets around it (protocol principle 2). A worker that records timings records the CPU too, so that comparisons can be guessed at.
- **Reversible stops do not hold a batch.** A stop a batch record reserves for him (a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, an interpreter output a rung cannot account for): "These don't need me now. They are reversible things I can review later. Don't block start of next batches on these." It lands, the push and the next batch go ahead, and it is listed for his review (the protocol's first hard rule). An output difference the untouched tree already shows from run to run, the test's verdict unchanged, is not a stop but a ledger row ("we had a rule too stringent because the spirit of the test is still held"); a rung's small items go to the ledger for review, not to him one per message.
- **Which decisions taken inside the work reach Pavol, and how.** A decision an agent takes is consequential when it reverses a decision on record, bends it or reads it anew; changes a line of the model program; touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation; chooses among ways the record does not settle; or cannot be undone. Everything else an agent decided is listed for later review, a rung's small items in the ledger, and holds nothing up. A consequential decision reaches Pavol one of three ways: asked before the work, a fork known in advance probed and put in the ask form before the batch is briefed; landed, then reviewed, one that can be undone landing, named in one line at the landing, listed in PLAN under the batch's list with the default that landed and put to Pavol later, one per message; or a stop that holds the work, one that cannot be undone or would act against Pavol's word, put at once. The `coordinator` skill states it (`decisions.md`, "Decisions and how they reach the curator").
- **The Fable rule.** "whenever it touches those three aspects of uh, library specification and implementation we are running the fable so if you use it sparingly I can pre-approve every such decision." The coordinator runs a Fable judgement without asking, sparingly, for a design question that touches two or more of the specification, the library and the implementation, once an Opus worker's evidence or list of ways is on file and the record has been searched and does not already settle it; he learns of it when the judgement is put to him in the ask form. He is asked first for any other Fable worker: a question about the coordinator's own conduct or a new kind of process choice, one whose recommendation would reverse a decision of his, or one where he wants Fable and Opus working independently. The standing pre-approvals: a judge's second ruling, and the top-tier reviews of the batch records.
- **One review after every batch.** "run the conformance review after every batch", combined with the process review into one pass, since "the amortized cost here is well worth the benefit": one Opus reviewer, reading only, does the conformance review, the process measures against `reviews/process-review-6b-7-7R.md` (misses by kind, those of items in the rung's own briefing, map use, briefing cost, re-measuring) and the routing check; the coordinator files what it finds in `PLAN.md` at the landing.
- **The phase-3 batches run on a standing go.** "I think you just carry on running the sequence of batches, I'll do the reset when I do it, If it stalls for a bit, I hope we'll recover without interruption. No need to complicate our runs with synchronization." And: "these are pre-approved. I want you to do autonomous overnight run." Each batch launches when the one before it has landed and its record is ready with no question open for him; a question a record raises goes to him first, except overnight, when it takes its recommended default and is listed for his review unless the default would reverse a decision of his, in which case that batch waits and the repair batch takes the slot; a run stalled by the limits is resumed with `resumeFromRunId`. A top-tier review in place of each coming batch record, in the form of `coordinator/climb-batch-7-review.md`, needs no further ask. The order is `PLAN.md`'s: batch 8 next. "Go" starts background work only; a batch run needs his explicit go, which for phase 3 this standing go is.
- **The new batch practice, and what he expects of it.** The practice after the post-mortem of the batch practice: the synthesis of its two reviews and both archaeologies, written into the script, its manual and the protocol, the script reviewed, a batch record rewritten to it and run on it, the landed batches' committed scratch cleaned in parallel, all built; of the post-mortem's four remaining questions, the output comparison is settled by his own position ("The suite's verdict is the check."), the merged-diff review stays by his word ("A blocking second review does not hold a green batch."), new tests are named by topic, as he asked of the files named after batches, and the cleaning ran by kind on his rule that only the reports and the changes to the repository stay; the rest of the review loops inside a batch (no second review, a judge and a repair only for a finding in code) are the synthesis's defaults, in force. "You can now redeem yourself by fixing this and, and, and showing me that you can be token efficient and not do bullshit jobs that you invented yourself." Every step spends the fewest workers the step needs and measures nothing the record already holds.
- **The gate's comparisons.** A comparison masks Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions, with every masked difference listed for him; the `testSystem` comparison is the sum of the four shards; a name comparison, red when a test that passed before is missing or failing, is a script change put to him on its own (parked, `PLAN.md`); row 366 waits; no route C entry goes into Proposed Features. A team test line the flat tower breaks is respelled keeping the value the test checks, no assertion deleted, every such line listed for him with its before and after.
- **The specification's examples join the gate at zero red.** `ant testSpecData`, the specification's extracted examples run under walk, joins the gate once its five red examples, each a reduction written without its element type, are green with row 424's F-bounded half (PLAN, batch 11); the examples are not respelled for walk and no list of known red examples is kept.
- **The order of the work after batch 10.** First the skills rewrite is finished: `fortress-repo`, `coordinator` and `cloud-container`, each read by him on the review page. Then the batch workflow is redesigned. Only then does the climb resume, with batch 11. The reason: the recent climbing was token-inefficient because the batches re-ran their costly parts, and those causes are what started the skill extraction; a batch run before both are done repeats them.
- **The gap ledger's form.** A row's status cell holds exactly one word of seven: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`; no second status and nothing in brackets; a row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED` and its notes say which half is fixed (D1 of `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md` section 4.5). The rewrite of the ledger is split among many small workers, each with a slice of rows it can hold in context, never one worker over the whole ledger; the duplicate search is a separate step before it, whose groups tell the rewrite which rows to join. The class cell is `kind (area)`, the area one of parser, walk, checker, codegen, runtime, library, prelude, specification, tests, tools; a specification citation gives the file and the section, a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; a row is at most 1,200 characters, the open rows cut to it by the rewrite; the full earlier text of every changed row is in one history file, `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md` (D2 to D5 at the proposal's defaults). The rows are sorted into topic sections, the rewrite's topical groups becoming the sections, each row keeping its number; a new row goes into the section its writer names, and row 83 becomes an eight-cell row in its section (D6). `explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py` owns the ledger's format and is the only way to write it (add with the template checked, note, close, duplicate, check); `facts-extract.sh` stays the one reader of every record, its ledger queries calling `ledger.py`'s parser. D7, numbering rows during parallel batches, is open.
